## Review action items from previous meeting

### How to handle security notifications ([discussion #331](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/tsc/discussions/331))

Rodrigo reminded everyone that Ry Jones (Linux Foundation) has set up a process for notifying the people responsible for an algorithm's implementation about a security advisory that concerns it. It is still manual, and as far as Rodrigo knows it has been used only once, by Douglas. He wanted to point out that the process exists and that the project should use it; later it could be made more automatic.

Michael asked how it works for someone who sees a report and wants to forward it to an upstream team. Rodrigo said Ry wrote documentation and a PR showing the process. In short, the upstream person's GitHub user is added to the specific advisory, so they can see everything in that advisory without seeing the others. Michael summarized: all that is needed is to know who the upstream contact is and add them as a collaborator on the advisory. Rodrigo confirmed.

> [!IMPORTANT]

Rodrigo then turned to the two architectural issues Michael raised some time ago. If the project decides to make these changes, it should at least announce them in the upcoming oqs-provider 0.13 release. He treated them as two independent discussions.

### Dropping algorithms that OpenSSL supports ([oqs-provider issue #821](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/oqs-provider/issues/821), [oqs-provider PR #870](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/oqs-provider/pull/870))

Rodrigo explained that, in his reading (and after discussing it with Douglas), the issue's title does not fully capture what it proposes. The current policy is that oqs-provider disables an algorithm only in those OpenSSL versions that ship it. For example, oqs-provider disables ML-KEM on OpenSSL 3.5 and later, but still offers it on 3.2. Issue #821 proposes that once an algorithm is in OpenSSL, oqs-provider stops offering it for all OpenSSL versions. Today this changes little, because OpenSSL no longer supports any version without post-quantum algorithms (3.5 is the oldest supported version). But it will matter in the future, for example when HQC is added to OpenSSL, so the policy is worth deciding.

**The two hybrid gaps.** Douglas asked about the table he had posted on [PR #870](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/oqs-provider/pull/870), which showed two hybrid combinations that the policy would drop; Michael had not responded to that point directly. Michael said he had stopped replying to anything mentioning hybrids in that thread, since Rodrigo had asked to keep the topics separate. Rodrigo said Douglas's question is in scope: these combinations would be dropped not because they are hybrids, but because OpenSSL implements them. Douglas summarized: under PR #870, SecP256r1MLKEM512 and MLKEM512X25519 would no longer be available. They do become available in later versions of OpenSSL, so there would be gaps on older supported versions, because the policy removes anything from oqs-provider once any version of OpenSSL supports it. Rodrigo agreed that this is exactly the decision to be made.

**Rationale.** Basil asked whether the rationale is general (OQS should not provide an implementation if OpenSSL has one) or technical (OpenSSL cannot handle two providers offering the same algorithm). Rodrigo said Michael should explain his original idea, but the benefit Rodrigo sees is technical simplicity: because OpenSSL does not handle two implementations of the same algorithm well, offering both creates a maintenance burden. If OpenSSL handled it, he would see no benefit in the proposal. Michael gave two further reasons. First, in OQS's relationship with OpenSSL, the project should not even give the impression of competing with it. Second, if users can end up with a configuration where they run ML-KEM, or any other algorithm, without knowing which implementation is underneath, that is dangerous, and the project should do everything it can to prevent it. Rodrigo said users also have to take some responsibility for knowing what they are using. Michael said that in security software, if you hand someone a gun to shoot themselves in the foot, the trigger should be made very safe.

**Users on older OpenSSL versions.** Douglas asked whether users will want to try new algorithms on older supported OpenSSL versions. For example, OpenSSL 4.3 is expected to bring HQC, but many people will still be on 3.5, 4.0 or 4.1; under the proposed policy they would have no way to try HQC. Rodrigo agreed that is possible.

**Alternative implementations.** Norm said that one benefit Cisco sees in OQS is that it offers an alternative implementation; Cisco tends never to want a single source for anything, and taking that away is a negative. Rodrigo asked what he meant by alternative. Norm said alternative implementations, particularly ones with autonomy and self-determination, give flexibility if they are ever needed; he sees this as agility rather than competition. Rodrigo said that self-determination does not really exist today, since OpenSSL does not allow two implementations to coexist and oqs-provider already disables algorithms that OpenSSL ships. The real difference the policy makes is the case Douglas raised. Norm said that, in OpenSSL's design, if both the default and FIPS providers are loaded and a caller asks for ML-KEM without a property query, there is no guarantee which provider supplies it, and OpenSSL says so openly. Rodrigo said a specific provider can be chosen. Norm agreed: users either call explicitly or set up their environment to guarantee what is called, so users carry some responsibility too.

Norm then pointed out that today the code still exists: someone could disable ML-KEM in OpenSSL's default provider and tweak oqs-provider to re-enable its own implementation. Under the proposed policy, that code would be removed from OQS. Rodrigo agreed this is possible today and had not thought of it; whether it remains possible depends on how removal is implemented. If an algorithm were only dropped from `generate.yml`, users could still add it back. Norm noted the project has not discussed whether removal means deleting the code or disabling it at build time. Michael said that once you start tweaking the default provider, you are no longer talking about oqs-provider's default behavior: re-enabling standard algorithms in oqs-provider would also be trivial.

**Options.** Douglas suggested there are three options, which should be written up properly after the meeting and discussed on GitHub, possibly leading to a vote:

1. Disable an algorithm or hybrid combination in oqs-provider if it is available in any supported version of OpenSSL (the proposal in #821/#870).
2. Disable it only in the OpenSSL versions that support it (the current policy).
3. A stronger option based on Norm's use case: even in OpenSSL versions that support an algorithm, allow it to be re-enabled in oqs-provider so that it can be used in place of OpenSSL's default provider.

Rodrigo suggested that the question may not be whether to disable but how: in a way that can or cannot be reversed through configuration, much as users can already choose which algorithms to compile into oqs-provider. Douglas suggested working through the options on GitHub until there is a shared understanding, and then moving towards a decision. Michael strongly recommended backing each option with code: discussion in theory could go on for a long time, while concrete PRs implementing each option would show their impact.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Action (Rodrigo):** Write up the three options for [oqs-provider issue #821](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/oqs-provider/issues/821) on GitHub and drive the discussion towards a decision, possibly a vote. Rodrigo noted he will have limited availability next week.

> [!NOTE]
> Michael recommended that each option be backed by a concrete PR so its impact can be evaluated.

### Splitting out hybrid support ([oqs-provider issue #847](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/oqs-provider/issues/847))

Rodrigo explained that oqs-provider does two things that could be independent: it binds liboqs to OpenSSL, and it implements hybrids. Issue #847 proposes splitting these into two providers. Architecturally, that seems logical to him. In his personal view, however, the discussion cannot be separated from where the hybrid provider would live. Experimental hybrid algorithms are experimental, and so fall within what OQS should cover. If OQS ended up doing less than it used to, that would be counterproductive for the project.

Michael restated his position. The [hybrid provider](https://github.com/baentsch/hybrid-provider) mirrors all of oqs-provider's hybrid functionality and goes beyond it, and is in that sense independent of OQS. He thinks it should stay independent, at least for some time, to see whether people contribute to it because of that independence. At the OpenSSL Conference, which Rodrigo and Norm also attended, the wolfSSL developers were impressed that it worked just as well with their provider as with the default provider, simple demo providers, and oqs-provider. Rodrigo said that working with other providers does not mean it has no place in OQS. OQS is not defined only by using liboqs code; its purpose is experimental post-quantum cryptography. Michael created the hybrid provider and so gets to decide its future, but in Rodrigo's view the independence question is not a technical one.

**User impact.** Norm said that from an architectural and user perspective, needing a second provider to do something oqs-provider already does complicates things. Even if hybrid code is not directly related to liboqs, removing it from oqs-provider is another loss. Rodrigo said the current structure is not simpler: he believes OQS should step up its work on hybrids, and expanding hybrid support in the current oqs-provider code base is very difficult because the code is so intertwined. A separate provider is not the only fix, but it makes architectural sense. Norm asked whether oqs-provider, originally designed for one purpose, could instead be expanded and cleaned up where there are inconsistencies or poor design, to account for changes in algorithms and how hybrids are used.

Douglas asked Norm to write up what adopting an additional provider for hybrid support would involve, both locally (installing another binary, editing configuration files) and for managing deployments, since he has little experience installing providers himself. Norm agreed. He said a large part of it is user experience, messaging and maintenance: Cisco has users running oqs-provider in its products, and would have to tell them that oqs-provider no longer does this and they now need a second provider. He added that although OQS is research-oriented, it also has other users.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Action (Norm):** Post a comment on [oqs-provider issue #847](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/oqs-provider/issues/847) describing what moving hybrid support to a separate provider would mean for Cisco and its users: installation, configuration, deployment management and user messaging.

**Experimental hybrids.** Basil agreed that the hybrid code in oqs-provider is hard to maintain and should be improved. He likes the architectural idea that hybrids can be built independently of the schemes, applying both to standardized algorithms and to the experimental ones in liboqs, and so can be a separate module or provider. His condition for an independent hybrid provider is that it allows free choice of any algorithm for prototyping, not only the standardized ML-KEM hybrids. Rodrigo agreed: experimenting with non-standard combinations is the interesting part for OQS, since standardized hybrids are already in OpenSSL. Michael said this already works in the hybrid provider: he has created composites and triple PQ/PQ/traditional combinations with FrodoKEM and others, in addition to everything oqs-provider does.

**Where would it live?** Rodrigo summarized two questions: whether to use two providers, which is Norm's concern; and, even if the TSC agreed on the architectural benefits of two providers (which Rodrigo personally supports), where the hybrid provider would live. Douglas clarified that the second question is whether the hybrid provider would be an OQS subproject. Rodrigo said yes: he thinks there is room for it in OQS because it is exactly what OQS does, and that going from supporting hybrids to not supporting them would be bad for OQS.

Michael asked why Rodrigo would consider OQS not supporting hybrids, since he has invited everyone in OQS to contribute to the hybrid provider. He also asked Douglas what he had meant in a recent comment by "some kind of formal tie" between the two projects. Douglas said he does not know what that would mean. The simplest option is for the hybrid provider to be a subproject, because the project knows what that structure looks like. If a formal relationship short of being a subproject is the only thing Michael will consider, the TSC would need to discuss what that means and whether it can work. Michael said he stands by his opinion for now but is willing to revisit it later, and wants to start working out what such a tie would mean. Technically, he has tried to ensure users would see no difference except improvements: better and faster code that does more while delivering everything oqs-provider does today. Douglas said a formal relationship is a matter of governance and process, not only technical functionality. Michael agreed, and said that is why he has not yet published a governance file for the hybrid provider: he wanted to hear at this meeting what matters to OQS.

**Relationship to the oqs-provider 0.13 release.** Douglas said this question will likely take a couple of months to resolve and cannot be settled in the current release cycle. Rodrigo proposed decoupling it from the oqs-provider 0.13 release, which should ship on time alongside liboqs 0.17. Once the question is resolved, the project could announce the outcome in a later release, cutting one specifically for the announcement if needed.

Michael asked who would own moving this forward and by when; he did not want it left hanging. Rodrigo committed to starting the discussions with the relevant parties, though not next week because of his PhD defense, and to holding a discussion before the holidays to see where things stand and what actions could bring it to a conclusion everyone is happy with. It will probably not be resolved before the holidays. The discussion needs to cover what independence for the hybrid provider would look like and how that relates to governance.

Michael said this delays something he had hoped would be settled earlier. He suggested that delaying oqs-provider 0.13 was another option, which might motivate a faster conclusion, and proposed discussing at a later meeting whether to delay the release if the question could be resolved first. Rodrigo said he does not need a release hanging in the balance to be motivated, and did not want to hold up a release the project had worked hard for. Douglas said he expects it to take months: it is probably the biggest decision in oqs-provider's history, it involves an external relationship of a kind OQS has never had, and a significant user has said a split would be problematic for their architecture. He does not think it should be rushed into two or three weeks even if there were capacity, and does not think it is worth delaying oqs-provider 0.13 just to include an announcement about a possible architecture change. If releases are used to highlight notable announcements, a point release could be cut when the time comes. Michael accepted this and asked Rodrigo to take it up.

**Outcome:** The discussion of issue #847 is decoupled from oqs-provider 0.13, which will be released on time alongside liboqs 0.17. Any outcome will be announced later, in a dedicated release if needed. Michael's position was noted.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Action (Rodrigo):** Start the discussion with the relevant parties on [oqs-provider issue #847](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/oqs-provider/issues/847): whether the hybrid provider would be an OQS subproject or have some other formal relationship with OQS, and what that would mean for governance and independence. Hold a discussion before the holidays.
